justice: The bridge deck allocates almost all visible space to multiple motor-vehicle lanes, while no dedicated pedestrian sidewalk is visible.
No bicycle lane, shoulder bikeway, or cycling markings can be seen, indicating unequal provision for non-motorized users.
Concrete barriers and guardrails line both sides of the elevated roadway, but there are no visible curb ramps, crosswalks, or barrier-free pedestrian access elements.
safety: Lane markings are clear and the asphalt surface appears smooth and well maintained, which supports predictable vehicle movement.
Tall streetlights are installed regularly along the median and roadside, improving basic roadway visibility after dark.
The roadway is wide and divided by a raised median, reducing head-on conflict risk, but the elevated high-speed setting offers little protection for pedestrians or cyclists if they were present.
livability: This is an elevated arterial or expressway environment dominated by fast-moving traffic lanes rather than human-scale public space.
There are no visible shops, benches, bus stops, or community-facing frontages along the roadway, limiting everyday street life.
Although distant greenery is visible beyond the barriers, the bridge itself provides almost no usable social or recreational space.
sustainability: Extensive tree cover and green land are visible on both sides of the elevated road corridor, which contributes some ecological value.
The infrastructure is clearly designed primarily for private motor traffic, with several wide lanes and no visible transit stop or protected cycle facility.
The raised median includes a narrow planted strip, but the overall cross-section remains highly car-oriented and material-intensive.
aesthetics: The open sky, expansive view, and continuous green edges create a visually pleasant long-distance outlook.
The roadway has a clean appearance with orderly lamp posts and crisp lane markings, giving a strong sense of visual tidiness.
The broad asphalt surface and concrete barriers are functional but monotonous, reducing architectural richness at street level.
comfort: There is almost no visible shade on the bridge deck itself, so exposed sun and heat gain would reduce thermal comfort for anyone outside a vehicle.
The pavement looks even and smooth for driving comfort, but there are no benches, refuges, or pedestrian amenities for physical comfort outside cars.
Wide separation from buildings and the open landscape may reduce enclosure stress, yet high-speed traffic conditions likely create psychological discomfort for non-drivers.
walkability: No continuous sidewalk is visible anywhere on the bridge, making basic pedestrian movement effectively unsupported.
There are no marked crossings, pedestrian signals, or refuge islands visible in the scene.
The elevated multi-lane high-speed road environment, bounded by concrete parapets and guardrails, is inhospitable and likely unusable for walking.
bikeability: No protected bike lane, painted cycle lane, or shared-lane marking is visible on the roadway.
The multi-lane elevated road appears designed for relatively high vehicle speeds, creating strong traffic stress for cyclists.
There is no visible bicycle parking, bicycle signalization, or barrier-separated cycling space along either edge of the bridge.
